What makes it even more frustrating is that the entire appointment still took about an hour, which is a completely normal amount of time for a long blowout. My hair is thick, but it is not curly and not difficult to style. If she knew she was running behind or did not have enough time to do the service properly, that should have been communicated before starting, or I should have been given the option to reschedule. Instead, I received a rushed service and was charged the full $70.

She barely went over my hair with a round brush, and the final result looked like it had just been rough dried instead of being an actual blowout. I left feeling like my time did not matter and that I paid $70 for something I did not even receive.

Please read before booking an appointment here ! My son and I traveled from Los Angeles to Sacramento he had a dreadlock re-twist appointment with Chantel. We paid $100 for the service, and the appointment was completed in less than 45 minutes. At the time, I thought the service seemed rushed, but I trusted that the work had been done correctly.

Unfortunately, within just two days, every single twist had unraveled. My son’s hair looked messy and undone, and this has never happened after any previous re-twist service. A re-twist should last significantly longer than 48 hours, especially when a customer is paying professional prices.

I contacted the salon owner Dr. T  to explain the situation and provide an opportunity to make things right. Instead of taking responsibility, I was told that Chantel is an independent contractor and that the salon could not do anything about it. The only solution offered was for us to return to Sacramento to have the service redone. Considering that we live in Los Angeles, this was not a practical or reasonable resolution.

What is most disappointing is not only the poor quality of the service but also the complete lack of accountability afterward. Customers do not book appointments based on a stylist's employment classification—they book with a business expecting professional service and support if something goes wrong. Passing responsibility to an independent contractor does not change the fact that the service failed almost immediately.

As a result, we are now forced to spend another $100 to have the work redone elsewhere. Businesses that value their reputation stand behind the services performed in their establishment and take customer concerns seriously. Unfortunately, that was not our experience here.

I rarely leave negative reviews, but I feel it is important for others to know what happened. Based on the quality of the work and the way this issue was handled, I cannot recommend this salon. If you are considering booking a re-twist service, I would strongly encourage you to do your research and choose a business that stands behind its work and values customer satisfaction.

My reply back: to Chantel

I would like to clarify a few points. It had not been four months since my son's last retwist—it had only been five weeks. Additionally, my son was not in any rush to leave. In fact, he told me that your staff was trying to leave, which may explain why he was not placed under the dryer.

Please do not attempt to shift responsibility onto the client. The issue is not my son's actions; the issue is the quality of the service provided. A retwist that completely unravels within two days is not acceptable and clearly indicates that the work was not performed thoroughly.

What is most disappointing is not only the poor quality of the service but also the unwillingness to take accountability. Rather than acknowledging the problem and standing behind your work, every effort has been made to place blame elsewhere. Businesses earn trust by taking responsibility when things go wrong, and unfortunately, that did not happen in this situation.

I understand that you do not offer refunds, although I strongly disagree with that policy given the outcome of this service. Regardless, I expect honesty and accountability. What happened to my son's hair was unacceptable, and the way this matter has been handled has only made the experience worse.

one_star_reviews.text:
Half Moon Bay has a nearly century-old bakery in an idyllic coastal town. Regrettably, the bakery appears to have lost interest in baking.

Few things inspire more confidence than an old bakery on the main street of a California coastal town.

Half Moon Bay Bakery has been here since 1927. The storefront possesses the sort of authenticity restaurant designers spend fortunes trying to counterfeit. You approach imagining butter, yeast, espresso and warm bread.

Instead, you encounter Doritos.

There is Red Bull.

And behind the counter sits that ancient symbol of European baking tradition: a microwave.

Normandy this is not.

The pastry case is plentiful, though plentiful should not be confused with fresh. Some cookies possess the structural integrity of roofing materials. Breads can seem tired. Pastries occasionally appear to have spent more time sightseeing in Half Moon Bay than the customers eating them.

Customers have noticed.

One patron described an overbaked loaf so hard it was effectively inedible—and said the bakery refused to exchange it. Another reported mold on pastries. A family whose post-Pumpkin Festival visit had been an annual tradition for more than 20 years said they received an old pie and stale bread.

Then there is the cake.

According to another customer, slices displayed in the bakery were recognized as Costco sheet cake.

One pauses.

There is nothing wrong with Costco cake. It performs an important civic function: feeding 40 children at a birthday party for roughly the price of parking in San Francisco.

But Costco does not operate beneath a sign reading BAKERY — EST. 1927.

A bakery selling Costco cake is rather like an Italian restaurant microwaving Stouffer’s lasagna and asking whether you’d care to see the wine list.

The problem isn’t the cake.

It’s the surrender.

A bakery makes one of civilization’s simplest promises: flour, butter, sugar, salt, fermentation, heat and skill.

We assume somebody woke at an indecent hour because dough required attention. We assume the croissant exists because somebody laminated it. We make the apparently heroic assumption that the cake was made by the establishment calling itself a bakery.

Half Moon Bay Bakery asks customers to supply much of the romance themselves.

Which is particularly baffling because Half Moon Bay is practically begging for a magnificent boulangerie.

Cold mornings. Tourists. Surfers. Cyclists. Affluent visitors coming over the hill. Locals wandering Main Street.

Put a genuinely exceptional bakery here and crowd control could become a matter for City Council.

Imagine baguettes emerging throughout the morning. Croissants shattering beside proper cappuccinos. Jambon-beurre wrapped for the beach. Fresh fruit tarts. Pastéis de nata honoring the Coastside’s Portuguese heritage.

This is not molecular gastronomy.

We are asking a bakery to bake.

The saddest reviews come from longtime customers. These people aren’t demanding reinvention. They’re mourning something they remember loving.

A historic bakery isn’t merely selling carbohydrates. It maintains rituals: the Friday loaf, morning coffee, Pumpkin Festival pie, the cookie remembered twenty years later.

Half Moon Bay Bakery is approaching a century on Main Street. That is genuinely remarkable.

But longevity alone does not confer greatness. A sourdough starter can survive for decades; we don’t let it manage the pastry case.

History is something an institution inherits. Legacy is something it earns.

And somewhere beneath the Doritos, tired pastries, Costco cake and gently humming microwave is a beautiful old bakery waiting for somebody to remember the difference.
